newsitem.title: CHINA: China gears up for Gore, tightens lid on dissidents.
newsitem.headline: China gears up for Gore, tightens lid on dissidents.

text.p: Families of jailed Chinese dissidents said on Wednesday they will be forced to leave Beijing or face intensified police surveillance ahead of U.S. Vice President Al Gore's visit next week.
Beijing is eager to ensure that nothing mars the visit by Gore, the most senior U.S. official to travel to China in eight years, dissidents said.
Gore is scheduled to visit March 24-28, part of painstaking efforts to restore ties damaged by friction over China's rival Taiwan.
Relatives of one prominent dissident now in jail said they would be shunted out of the Chinese capital for a prison visit this weekend.
"Police have arranged for us (family) to go visit him (in prison) this weekend," said a relative, who asked not to be further identified.
China has jailed most of its small band of active dissidents. In the past, it has moved to isolate dissidents and their relatives during visits by U.S. officials or on other sensitive occasions.
Chu Hailan, wife of veteran dissident Liu Nianchun who is serving a three-year sentence at a labour camp, said she expected police surveillance to tighten.
"Surveillance was tight when the National People's Congress (parliament) was in session...I'm certain they (security agents) will return when the U.S. vice president comes next week," Chu said.
"I guess they're afraid I would meet them (U.S. officials) and speak out," she said.
Other dissidents' relatives echoed her concerns.
"We should see police step up their activities in the next few days," said a relative of another dissident.
Human rights abuses in China have long been a sore spot in Sino-U.S. relations, particularly in the years after China called in the army to crush a student-led democracy movement in Beijing in 1989.
In its annual report on human rights, the U.S. State Department accused Beijing of effectively silencing public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.
China considers dissidents like Wei Jingsheng, dubbed the father of China's modern democracy movement and a nominee of the Nobel Peace Prize, as common criminals.
Hong Kong's Sing Tao newspaper said on Wednesday that Chinese authorities have offered ahead of Gore's visit to release dissident Wang Dan on condition that he leaves China for a third country.

Wang, a former student leader of the 1989 demonstrations, has agreed to China's condition and was expected to be released soon, the daily said, quoting an official and a source close to the dissident.
Asked to comment on the newspaper report, Wang's father, Wang Xianzeng, said: "I haven't heard any news. He's still in prison."
